clinicalPearls: A benign cystic neoplasm composed of glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium, with a very low risk of malignant transformation
More common in older women and often discovered incidentally
The classic microcystic form has numerous small cysts producing a honeycomb appearance, sometimes with a central stellate scar and calcification
The cyst fluid is typically low in CEA, helping to distinguish it from mucinous cystic lesions
Less common macrocystic (oligocystic) variants can mimic mucinous neoplasms on imaging and are harder to characterise
Because it is benign, asymptomatic serous cystadenoma can usually be managed by observation once the diagnosis is confident
Resection is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, large or rapidly enlarging lesions, or symptoms from mass effect
reference.pathophysiology: Serous cystadenomas arise from centroacinar or ductal epithelial cells and are lined by a single layer of glycogen-rich, cuboidal serous epithelium that secretes thin, watery fluid. The cells proliferate to form clusters of cysts, most often numerous small locules separated by thin fibrous septa that radiate from a central scar, giving the characteristic microcystic and honeycomb morphology; calcification may develop within the scar. Many of these tumours are associated with inactivation of the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, and lesions are common in von Hippel-Lindau disease. The epithelium lacks the mucinous phenotype and malignant potential of mucinous cystic neoplasms, so the fluid CEA is characteristically low and malignant change is exceedingly rare.
additionalDifferentials: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to identify the microcystic pattern and central scar
Endoscopic ultrasound to characterise the cysts and septa
Fine-needle aspiration for cyst fluid CEA (characteristically low) and cytology
Cyst fluid glucose assessment, which tends to be high in serous lesions
MRCP to confirm absence of main duct communication
Genetic evaluation for von Hippel-Lindau disease when clinically suggested
redFlags: Atypical or macrocystic morphology that cannot be distinguished from a mucinous neoplasm
Rapid growth or a very large lesion causing compressive symptoms
An enhancing solid component prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Obstructive jaundice or duct dilatation from mass effect
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent because malignant transformation is very rare; most lesions can be observed safely, and surgical resection, when required for symptoms or uncertainty, is curative.
pitfalls: Mistaking an oligocystic (macrocystic) serous cystadenoma for a mucinous neoplasm and over-treating, or the reverse and under-treating
Over-reliance on imaging alone without confirmatory low cyst fluid CEA
Attempting aspiration of a highly vascular microcystic lesion with risk of bleeding
Recommending resection of a confidently benign, asymptomatic lesion
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
European evidence-based guidelines on pancreatic cystic neoplasms
WHO classification of tumours of the digestive system
management: Manage a confidently diagnosed asymptomatic lesion by observation with periodic surveillance imaging, given the very low malignant potential
Undertake surgical resection appropriate to site, such as distal pancreatectomy, enucleation, or pancreatoduodenectomy, for symptomatic, large, enlarging, or diagnostically uncertain lesions
Characterise the cyst with endoscopic ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration, using low fluid CEA and high fluid glucose to distinguish it from mucinous neoplasms
Manage mass-effect complications such as biliary or gastric outlet obstruction
Evaluate for von Hippel-Lindau disease when clinically suggested, with genetic counselling and surveillance if confirmed
Refer to a hepatobiliary and pancreatology multidisciplinary team for the resection-versus-observation decision

Microcystic honeycomb with central scar and low fluid CEA?
